reason: The sources provide over 15 multi-sourced facts detailing the scale, discovery, composition, and disputed cosmic destruction of the Pillars of Creation.
story: On April 1, 1995, the Hubble Space Telescope captured one of the most iconic views in human history: the Pillars of Creation. Located roughly 6,500 light-years away in the Eagle Nebula, these immense towers of cold molecular hydrogen gas and dust span four light-years from base to tip—roughly 24 trillion miles high. Inside these columns, dense pockets nicknamed EGGs, or Evaporating Gaseous Globules, act as cosmic incubators where embryonic stars ignite. But creation comes with destruction. Intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from nearby massive stars are violently sandblasting the gas away in a process called photoevaporation. In fact, infrared observations from the Spitzer Space Telescope suggested a nearby supernova blast wave might have already wiped the pillars out 6,000 years ago. Because of the vast distance light must travel, humanity won't see whether they survived or vanished for another thousand years.
angle: These towering four-light-year-tall cosmic columns may have already been destroyed 6,000 years ago by a supernova shockwave, but light travel time means we won't see it happen for another thousand years.

claims.claim: The Pillars of Creation are towering columns of interstellar gas and dust located within the Eagle Nebula (Messier 16).
The Eagle Nebula is situated in the constellation Serpens.
The pillars lie at an interstellar distance of roughly 6,500 to 7,000 light-years from Earth.
The tallest, leftmost pillar spans approximately four light-years from its base to its tip.
The original photograph was captured by the Hubble Space Telescope on April 1, 1995.
The original Hubble observations were led by Arizona State University astronomers Jeff Hester and Paul Scowen.
The pillars are composed of cool molecular hydrogen gas and interstellar dust.
The pillars are shaped and eroded by ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from nearby hot, massive stars in a process called photoevaporation.
Dense pockets of gas inside the pillars where embryonic stars form are designated EGGs, an acronym for Evaporating Gaseous Globules.
When photoevaporation uncovers an EGG, the forming star abruptly stops growing as it is separated from the surrounding reservoir of gas.
The 1995 photograph was captured using Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 (WFPC2).
The colors in the composite image correspond to atomic emission lines: green for hydrogen, red for singly ionized sulfur, and blue for doubly ionized oxygen.
The photograph became a massive cultural phenomenon, appearing on everyday commercial items such as t-shirts and coffee mugs.
In January 2015, astronomers unveiled a sharper, wider revisit photograph taken by Hubble to celebrate the telescope's 25th anniversary.
Infrared images from the Spitzer Space Telescope suggested a supernova shockwave may have destroyed the pillars roughly 6,000 years ago.
Because of the 7,000-year light travel time to Earth, evidence of the pillars' destruction from a supernova shockwave would not be visible for another 1,000 years.
Astronomer Stephen Reynolds disputed the supernova destruction model, arguing that stellar winds heated the dust and the pillars are eroding more gradually.
NASA's James Webb Space Telescope re-imaged the Pillars of Creation in infrared light in 2022, capturing active star formation at the tips.
NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory surveyed the area to observe young stars and protostars via X-ray emissions.

disputed: Supernova destruction vs. gradual stellar wind erosion: Nicolas Flagey and Spitzer data suggested a supernova blast wave destroyed the pillars 6,000 years ago (visible from Earth in ~1,000 years), while Stephen Reynolds pointed out a lack of expected radio and X-ray emission and argued massive stellar winds are eroding them gradually instead. Script should attribute both interpretations clearly.
Distance to the nebula: Some sources state 6,500 light-years while others cite 7,000 light-years. Script should state the approximate range of 6,500 to 7,000 light-years.
